muse_spark_1.3/001: The strategy is optimal misère Nim for 4 piles where the last take loses. If all piles are 0/1 the position is winning iff the number of 1s is even, so remove one 1. If exactly one pile is >1 with k ones, all such positions are winning: with k even reduce the big pile to 1, with k odd remove it, leaving an odd number of 1s which is losing for the opponent. This is the opposite of normal Nim and traps normal-play opponents. If at least two piles are >1, misère coincides with normal Nim: P-positions are xor==0. From xor!=0 move to xor==0 by replacing a pile p with p^xor. From xor==0, losing with perfect play, try to trap: with exactly 2 big piles reduce one big to 1 to leave a single-big position where normal vs misère differ; with 3+ big take 1 from the largest to prolong the game. A safe fallback guarantees a legal move.
muse_spark_1.3/002: The strategy is perfect misère Nim for 4 piles where last-take loses. If all piles are 0/1 with `k` ones, the position is winning iff `k` is even. If exactly one pile `H>1` with `k` ones, the position is always winning: take all of `H` if `k` is odd to leave `k` ones, otherwise leave 1 to leave `k+1` ones, in both cases leaving an odd number of ones for the opponent. If at least two piles are `>1`, the P-positions are exactly xor `==0`, same as normal Nim, and the winning move is the normal xor-zeroing move, which can never degenerate to all-small or single-big-zero-xor. From a losing xor-zero position any move loses versus perfect play, so we trap a normal-Nim opponent by moving to a single-big position with even number of ones where normal and misère moves differ, otherwise we prolong by taking 1 from the largest pile. Among multiple winning xor-moves we keep the maximum stones to give the opponent more chances to err. A safe fallback guarantees a legal move.
muse_spark_1.3/003: The strategy is optimal misère Nim for 4 piles where taking the last object loses. Let xor be the nim-sum and k the number of piles larger than 1. If k==0 all piles are 0/1 and the position is winning iff the number of 1s is even, so take one whole 1-pile. If k==1 with big pile B and s ones, winning play must leave all piles <=1 with an odd number of 1s for the opponent, so reduce B to 1 when s is even and remove B completely when s is odd. If k>=2 normal Nim applies: with xor!=0 move to xor==0 by replacing pile p with p^xor, which provably stays with k>=2; with xor==0 the position is losing against perfect play, so move to a k==1 trap to exploit normal-play opponents, otherwise take minimally from the largest pile. A safe fallback always returns a legal move.
muse_spark_1.3/004:
The strategy is optimal misère Nim for 4 piles with trap play from losing positions.
Win/loss is: 0 large piles (>1) is losing iff odd number of ones, 1 large pile is always winning, 2+ large piles is losing iff xor==0. From a winning position take to a losing position, keeping the most stones to prolong the game. With one large pile take it to 0 if odd ones else to 1. From a losing 2-large position move to 1-large to trap normal-play opponents. Otherwise minimise opponent immediate winning ratio wins/total to beat random play. Fallback always returns a legal move.
muse_spark_1.3/005:
The strategy is optimal misère Nim for 4 piles where last-take loses.

If all piles are 0/1 the position with an even number of 1's is winning (xor==0), with an odd number is losing. The winning move removes one whole 1-pile to flip parity to odd.

If some pile is >1, P-positions coincide with normal Nim: xor==0 is losing, xor!=0 is winning.
With at least two piles >1 the winning move is the normal Nim move to xor 0, which must leave at least two piles >1 and is therefore a misère P-position.
With exactly one pile L>1 and s piles of size 1, xor can never be 0 and the position is always N. The win is to move the large pile to 0 if s is odd and to 1 if s is even, leaving an odd number of 1's, i.e. an all-1 P-position.
From a losing xor==0 position any move loses against perfect play, so play a stalling move that keeps at least two piles >1 if possible to maximize complexity.
